items.stem: An operator types `ls -la` to see hidden files in long format. Which two single-letter options does that one hyphenated word actually expand to?

options.text: `-l` and `-a`, clustered behind one leading hyphen
options.why: Short options take one hyphen each and may be clustered behind a single hyphen, so `-la` is exactly `-l -a`.

options.text: `-l` and `-A`, since a clustered letter is read case-insensitively
options.why: Clustering does not fold case; `-a` and `-A` are different options with different meanings for dotfiles.

options.text: A single long option spelled with one leading hyphen
options.why: A single hyphen introduces a cluster of short options; a long option always needs two hyphens.

options.text: `-l` only, with the trailing `a` passed on as a separate operand
options.why: Every letter after the single hyphen is parsed as its own clustered option, not as text handed to the command.

items.rationale: Short options take one hyphen and a single letter, and may be clustered behind one hyphen, so `ls -la` is exactly `ls -l -a`. Long options take two hyphens and a whole word and may never be clustered this way. Written without clustering, the same request is `ls -l`.

verification.reasoning: Key checked against POSIX.1-2024 Utility Conventions Guideline 5, which states that one or more options without option-arguments should be accepted when grouped behind one '-' delimiter, so `-la` is exactly `-l -a`. o2: nothing in the guidelines folds case, and ls(1) documents `-a` (do not ignore entries starting with .) and `-A` (do not list implied . and ..) as distinct options with distinct meanings. o3: Guideline 3 restricts an option name to a single alphanumeric character behind one hyphen; the two-hyphen long form is a GNU extension, so a one-hyphen long option is not a thing. o4: every letter in a cluster is parsed as its own option, not handed on as text. No distractor is defensible. Citation strengthened at concept level with ls(1).

items.stem: A script written for a GNU/Linux server uses `ls --all` to show dotfiles, then is copied to run unmodified on a macOS workstation. What happens on macOS?

options.text: The BSD `ls` on macOS rejects `--all`, though `-a` still works there
options.why: Long options are a GNU coreutils convention rather than a POSIX requirement, and the BSD `ls` shipped with macOS does not implement this one.

options.text: It runs identically, since long options are part of the POSIX utility syntax
options.why: POSIX defines only single-character options; long options like `--all` are a GNU extension with no portability guarantee.

options.text: It silently lists nothing, because macOS treats an unknown flag as matching zero files
options.why: An unrecognized option is reported as an error, not treated as a filter that matches nothing.

options.text: It behaves the same as `ls -A`, since macOS maps unknown long options to the nearest short one
options.why: There is no such fallback mapping; an unsupported long option is simply rejected.

items.rationale: The GNU coreutils `ls --all` is equivalent to `-a`, but long options are a GNU convention, not a POSIX one, so a BSD or macOS userland can reject them outright even while the short forms keep working.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The item turns on a claim about the BSD `ls` shipped with macOS, and not one cited source (LF objectives, POSIX Utility Conventions, GNU coreutils manual) documents that implementation at all — a 'right topic, wrong document' citation of exactly the class this wave was told to hunt. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: added `apple-ls-1` (Apple's own ls(1) page) at concept level and re-checked. Apple's ls(1) SYNOPSIS is `ls [-@ABCFGHILOPRSTUWabcdefghiklmnopqrstuvwxy1%,] [--color=when] [-D format] [file ...]`; `--color` is the only long option on the page and `--all` appears nowhere, so `ls --all` is rejected while `-a` is listed and works. POSIX Guideline 3 confirms o2's premise is false: an option name should be a single alphanumeric character, so long options are outside the POSIX syntax. o3 and o4 assert behaviours (silent zero-match filtering, automatic long-to-short fallback) that appear in no implementation and are contradicted by BSD getopt reporting an illegal option. Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: A directory contains a file literally named `-r`, and a command needs to operate on it without the shell reading `-r` as an option. Which construct marks the end of options so a following operand starting with a hyphen is treated as a filename?

options.text: A standalone `--` placed before the filename
options.why: A double hyphen on its own is the end-of-options marker; every word after it is treated as an operand even if it starts with a hyphen.

options.text: Wrapping the filename in single quotes
options.why: Quoting stops the shell from expanding the word, but the command itself would still parse a leading hyphen as an option.

options.text: Escaping the leading hyphen with a backslash
options.why: A backslash escapes shell metacharacters; a hyphen has no special meaning to the shell, so this changes nothing about how the command parses its arguments.

options.text: Prefixing the filename with `./`
options.why: Writing `./-r` does keep the argument from beginning with a hyphen, but it works by rewriting the pathname itself rather than by marking where options stop, and it does nothing for an operand that is not a pathname.

items.rationale: A double hyphen on its own marks the end of options, so any operand after it — including one that starts with a hyphen — is treated as an operand rather than parsed as an option.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. o4's `why` stated that a leading `./` 'does make the word start with a slash instead of a hyphen' — false on its face: `./-r` starts with a dot, not a slash. A distractor rationale that misdescribes the very construct it is correcting is a false lesson. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o4's `why` rewritten to say the `./` prefix rewrites the pathname rather than marking the end of options. Key re-checked against POSIX.1-2024 Utility Conventions Guideline 10: 'The first -- argument that is not an option-argument should be accepted as a delimiter indicating the end of options. Any following arguments should be treated as operands, even if they begin with the '-' character.' o2 is true as stated (quoting suppresses shell processing, not the utility's own option parsing) and o3 is true (a hyphen is not a shell metacharacter, so backslash-escaping it changes nothing). No distractor answers the stem.

items.stem: An operator needs the five-field time syntax used inside a crontab file, not the usage of the `crontab` command itself. Which invocation opens the correct manual page?

options.text: `man 5 crontab`, which asks for the file-format section explicitly
options.why: Section 5 documents file formats and configuration files, and a leading section number selects it directly.

options.text: `man crontab`, which opens whichever section is searched first
options.why: The default section search order reaches section 1 before section 5, so this opens the command page, not the file-format page.

options.text: `man -k crontab`, which searches page descriptions for the keyword
options.why: That searches the short descriptions in the manual index and returns a list of matches; it does not open the file-format page directly.

options.text: `info crontab`, since Texinfo manuals are organised into the same numbered sections as man
options.why: Texinfo manuals are not divided into man's numbered sections, so this does not target the file-format documentation specifically.

items.rationale: Manual sections are fixed, and section 5 covers file formats and configuration files while section 1 covers user commands. `man 5 crontab` asks for the file-format page explicitly, which is the one with the five time fields.

verification.reasoning: Key and every distractor checked against man(1). man(1)'s section table lists '5 File formats and conventions, e.g. /etc/passwd', and the SYNOPSIS shows `man [[section] page ...]`, so `man 5 crontab` selects the file-format page directly. o2 is refuted by man(1) DEFAULTS: 'The order of sections to search ... By default it is as follows: 1 n l 8 3 0 2 3type 5 4 9 6 7' combined with 'to show only the first page found, even if page exists in several sections' — section 1 is reached before section 5, so bare `man crontab` opens the command page. o3: man(1) documents `-k` as equivalent to apropos(1), a description search returning a list, not a page. o4: Texinfo manuals carry no man section numbers. crontab(5) confirms the five time fields the stem describes. Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: `apropos ssh` prints "nothing appropriate" on a server that clearly has OpenSSH installed, yet `man ssh` opens a page without trouble. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The manual index that `apropos` searches has not been built
options.why: `apropos` and `man -k` search a prebuilt index of page descriptions, generated by `mandb`, and that index can be missing or stale even when the pages themselves are present.

options.text: OpenSSH ships no man pages, only a `--help` summary
options.why: OpenSSH does ship man pages, and the scenario states `man ssh` already opens one successfully.

options.text: `apropos` only searches section 8 administration pages, and `ssh` lives in section 1
options.why: `apropos` searches descriptions across all sections; it is not restricted to section 8.

options.text: The keyword needs to be quoted, since `apropos` otherwise expands it as a glob
options.why: `apropos` takes the keyword as a plain operand; there is no glob expansion involved in the failure described.

items.rationale: `man -k` and `apropos` search the same prebuilt index of page descriptions rather than the page bodies, so an unbuilt or stale `mandb` index produces "nothing appropriate" even though the page itself opens with `man` directly.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The key's load-bearing claim is that `apropos` searches a prebuilt index generated by `mandb`. Neither cited source carried it: man(1) mentions mandb only in passing (`-u` 'update its database caches ... it is normally better to run mandb(8)') and man-pages(7) is about writing man pages and says nothing about apropos at all. This is the same defect class as the confirmed `man-apropos` cited for `man -k` finding, inverted. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: added `man-apropos` at concept level. apropos(1) states directly: 'The database searched by apropos is updated by the mandb program. Depending on your installation, this may be run by a periodic cron job, or may need to be run manually after new manual pages have been installed', and its FILES section names the index database caches. That is the key, verbatim. o2 is contradicted by the stem itself. o3: apropos(1) has no section restriction (it has `-s` to add one), so it is not limited to section 8. o4: apropos(1) takes the keyword as a plain operand and warns only that shell metacharacters may need quoting — no glob expansion produces this failure. Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: A container image ships a stripped-down set of binaries with no man pages installed at all. `man ls` fails with "No manual entry", but `ls --help` still prints a usage summary. Why does `--help` still work?

options.text: Its output is compiled into the binary itself, unlike a man page, which is a separate installed file
options.why: A man page is a separate installed file under the manual hierarchy — man(1) lists `/usr/share/man` among its FILES — so a stripped image can leave it out entirely, while the `--help` text is produced by the program itself and ships inside the binary.

options.text: `--help` reads the same source file `info` uses, which the image keeps for licensing reasons
options.why: `info` manuals are Texinfo files, a different format from a compiled-in `--help` summary, and neither depends on the other.

options.text: The image substitutes `apropos` output whenever a man page is missing, falling back to the short description instead
options.why: `apropos` searches the manual index database, which a stripped image would be missing along with the pages themselves, and it plays no part in producing a program's `--help` output.

options.text: Both `man` and `--help` actually failed, and the terminal replayed a cached result
options.why: The scenario states `--help` printed a usage summary, so it did not fail, and no such caching or replay happens here.

items.rationale: `--help` output is compiled into the binary, so it works even where man pages are separately installed files a minimal image chose to omit.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. Two defects. (1) o3 was self-refuting: its text ended '— reasonable on its face, but not how this actually works', announcing its own wrongness to the reader. (2) No cited source documented the key: man-pages(7) and man(1) say nothing about `--help`, and the LF objectives page is not documentation. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o3's trailing giveaway replaced with a plausible false mechanism (a fallback to the short description); `man-ls-1` added at concept level; the key's `why` rewritten to rest on what the sources actually say — man(1) FILES lists '/usr/share/man A global manual page hierarchy', establishing the page as a separate installed file, and ls(1) documents `--help` as an option of the program itself. o2 is false: `info` manuals are Texinfo, an unrelated format. o4 is contradicted by the stem. Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: A backup script works perfectly when run by hand at the prompt, but fails to find its input file when the same script runs from a cron job. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The script uses a relative path, and cron starts it from a different working directory
options.why: A relative path resolves from the current working directory, which is a per-process attribute; cron does not inherit the interactive shell's directory.

options.text: Cron strips environment variables the script needs to build the path, since cron jobs run with a stripped-down `PATH` and no interactive shell profile sourced
options.why: Cron does run a minimal environment, but the scenario describes a path lookup failure, not a missing variable.

options.text: The input file was renamed with a different case between the two runs
options.why: Nothing in the scenario indicates a name change; the same script works by hand and fails only from cron, which points at the environment, not the filename.

options.text: Cron always runs scripts with `$PWD` unset, so any path lookup fails outright
options.why: Every process has a current working directory, and the shell cron starts sets `PWD` for itself; a lookup does not fail 'outright' for want of that variable, and the resulting error would differ from the one described.

items.rationale: A relative path is resolved from the calling process's current working directory. Cron, a systemd unit, or a container entrypoint typically start with a different working directory than an interactive shell, so a relative path that works by hand can silently name the wrong file, or none, elsewhere.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. o4's `why` answered a different proposition than o4's text: the text claimed `$PWD` is unset, the `why` replied that cron 'sets a working directory just like any other process' — conflating the shell variable with the process attribute, so the correction did not actually correct the stated error. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o4's `why` rewritten to address the variable and the process attribute separately. Key re-checked against path_resolution(7): 'If the pathname does not start with the / character, the starting lookup directory of the resolution process is the current working directory of the process' — a per-process attribute, so a relative path resolves differently under a different cwd. crontab(5) confirms cron supplies its own environment (SHELL=/bin/sh, HOME and LOGNAME from /etc/passwd) rather than inheriting the interactive shell's context. o2 is true about cron's minimal environment but does not match the described symptom; o3 is ruled out by the scenario. Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: A directory was reached by following a symlink. Which command reports the physical location with the symlink resolved, rather than the logical path the shell has been tracking as text?

options.text: Running `pwd -P` to print the physical path with symlinks resolved
options.why: `-P` prints the physical path with symlinks resolved; plain `pwd` prints the logical path the shell tracked as it followed the symlink.

options.text: Running `pwd -L`, the logical form and also the default behaviour
options.why: `-L` is the logical form, and it is also the default; it returns the same symlink-preserving path plain `pwd` already gives.

options.text: `cd -P`, run with no other arguments
options.why: `cd -P` changes directory while resolving symlinks along the way; it does not print the current location the way `pwd` does.

options.text: `ls -ld` on the current directory, which prints the directory's own resolved physical path in the listing
options.why: A long listing of the directory entry shows its mode, links, owner, size and name; it never prints the working directory's own pathname, resolved or otherwise.

items.rationale: The shell tracks the working directory as a text string in `$PWD`, and plain `pwd` prints that logical path, following whatever symlinks were used to arrive. `pwd -P` instead prints the physical path with all symlinks resolved.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. Two defects. (1) o4 was self-refuting — '`ls -l` on the current directory — reasonable on its face, but not how this actually works'. (2) The key turns on `pwd -P`, and no cited source documented it: path_resolution(7) does not mention pwd, and the POSIX Shell Command Language chapter is about shell grammar, not the pwd utility. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o4 rewritten as a concrete false claim about `ls -ld`; `man-pwd-1` and `man-bash-1` added at concept level. pwd(1): '-L, --logical use PWD from environment, even if it contains symlinks; -P, --physical resolve all symlinks'. bash(1)'s pwd builtin: 'The pathname printed contains no symbolic links if the -P option is supplied ...; if the -L option is used, the pathname printed may contain symbolic links', and bash's `cd` behaves as if `-L` had been supplied when neither is given — which is why o2 is true as written and is not a second key. o3 is true as stated: bash(1) documents `cd -P` as changing directory while resolving symlinks; it prints nothing. Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: A shell script ends with the line `cd /var/log`, and the operator expects their interactive shell to land in `/var/log` after the script finishes. Why does the interactive shell stay exactly where it was?

options.text: The script runs as a child process, and a child cannot change its parent's working directory
options.why: The current working directory is a per-process attribute inherited at fork time; a child changing its own copy has no effect on the parent's.

options.text: `cd` inside a script is silently disabled for security reasons, since a script is assumed to run in a restricted, non-interactive shell that cannot change directories
options.why: `cd` works normally inside a script; it changes the script's own working directory, it just cannot propagate that change back to the caller.

options.text: The path `/var/log` does not exist on most systems, so the `cd` fails quietly
options.why: `/var/log` is a standard, near-universal directory; the described behaviour happens whether or not the target exists, because it is about process inheritance.

options.text: Only `cd -` can change a directory permanently; a bare `cd path` is temporary by design
options.why: There is no such distinction; `cd -` simply returns to the previous directory and is subject to the same per-process scoping as any other `cd`.

items.rationale: A script runs as a child process, and the working directory is a per-process attribute. The child's `cd` changes only its own copy, which disappears when the child exits, leaving the calling shell exactly where it was.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The key rests on the working directory being a per-process attribute a child cannot write back to its parent, and none of the three cited sources documented that: path_resolution(7) describes how a pathname is resolved, not process inheritance, and the POSIX Shell Command Language chapter does not cover `cd`'s scope. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: `man-bash-1` added at concept level. bash(1)'s cd builtin: 'Change the current directory to dir ... If the directory change is successful, cd sets the value of the PWD environment variable to the new directory name' — the shell executing the script, and only that shell. path_resolution(7) supplies the other half: the starting lookup directory is 'the current working directory of the process', i.e. per-process. o2 is false (cd is not disabled in scripts, and its `why` says so correctly); o3 is false (`/var/log` is standard, and the behaviour is independent of the target existing); o4 is false (bash(1) documents `-` only as 'converted to $OLDPWD before attempting the directory change', with no permanence distinction). Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: A crontab carries the environment line `ARCHIVE=~/archive`, and the job that later uses `$ARCHIVE` fails because the path stays literally `~/archive`. A `..` written into that same value resolves normally. Why does the tilde fail where `..` does not?

options.text: `~` is shell syntax, and cron assigns that line's value verbatim without a shell
options.why: crontab(5) defines an environment setting as `name = value`, with the text after the equals sign taken as the value and cron assigning it itself. bash(1) expands a tilde only when it begins an unquoted word the shell is parsing, and the shell does not rescan the result of a later parameter expansion for tildes.

options.text: Cron treats `~` as a comment character and discards the rest of the line
options.why: crontab(5) makes only a line whose first non-whitespace character is a pound sign a comment; a tilde carries no comment meaning and the value is passed through intact.

options.text: `..` is also unreliable in a crontab, so the job likely fails for a different reason entirely
options.why: path_resolution(7) states that every directory has the entries `.` and `..` with their conventional meanings, so `..` is resolved by the kernel in any pathname, including one cron hands to a program.

options.text: `~` only expands inside double quotes, and the crontab line was unquoted
options.why: bash(1) requires the tilde to be unquoted, so quoting suppresses expansion rather than enabling it, and crontab(5) says quotes around a value only preserve leading and trailing whitespace.

items.rationale: Tilde expansion is performed by the shell before a command runs. Files like a crontab or a systemd unit are read directly, with no shell involved, so a tilde written there stays literal, while `.` and `..` are real directory entries the kernel resolves wherever a path is accepted.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The item's premise was factually wrong, not merely under-cited. As written it placed the tilde in a crontab job's command and claimed 'cron does not read that file with a shell'. crontab(5) says the opposite of the load-bearing half: 'The entire command portion of the line, up to a newline or a "%" character, will be executed by /bin/sh or by the shell specified in the SHELL variable of the cronfile.' A tilde in the command field therefore IS expanded, by that shell, and the authored scenario would not fail. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: the stem was moved to the one part of a crontab cron parses itself — an environment-assignment line — where the behaviour the item teaches is real and documented. crontab(5): 'An environment setting is of the form: name = value where the white spaces around the equal-sign (=) are optional, and any subsequent non-leading white spaces in value is a part of the value assigned to name. The value string may be placed in quotes ... to preserve leading or trailing white spaces.' No expansion step exists there, and bash(1) confirms tilde expansion needs 'a word [that] begins with an unquoted tilde character' in a shell — and that 'the results of tilde expansion are treated as if they were quoted', so no re-expansion of a variable's value occurs either. path_resolution(7) supplies the `..` half. All four options rewritten against those two pages; no distractor is defensible and none announces its own wrongness.

items.stem: An operator `cd`s into a directory through a symlink and then runs `cd ..`. The result is not the directory that physically contains the symlink's target. What explains this?

options.text: Bash's `cd ..` is logical by default, stripping the last component of `$PWD` as text
options.why: The shell tracks `$PWD` as a string and strips its last component textually, so after arriving through a symlink the logical parent can differ from the physical one; `cd -P ..` follows the physical structure instead.

options.text: The symlink itself was deleted between the two commands, which makes the shell fall back to the physical parent
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests the symlink vanished, and removing it would not retroactively change the `$PWD` string the shell had already recorded; the discrepancy is the ordinary result of logical-versus-physical resolution.

options.text: `..` at the root of a symlinked mount always resolves to `/` regardless of position
options.why: That special case applies only to `..` evaluated at the actual filesystem root, not to an ordinary directory reached through a symlink elsewhere in the tree.

options.text: Only `~` behaves this way; `..` always matches the kernel's physical parent
options.why: Bash's default `cd ..` is explicitly logical, tracking `$PWD` as text, which is exactly why it can diverge from the kernel's physical parent.

items.rationale: In bash, `cd ..` is logical by default: the shell strips the last component from `$PWD` textually. After arriving through a symlink, that can land somewhere different from what `..` physically points at on disk; `cd -P ..` follows the physical structure instead.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. o2 was self-refuting — its text ended 'though that is not what actually happens in practice', telling the reader it was wrong before they reasoned about it. The key was also uncited: nothing in path_resolution(7), the FHS or the LF objectives page documents bash's logical `cd`. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o2's giveaway clause replaced with a concrete false mechanism, and `man-bash-1` added at concept level. bash(1)'s cd builtin is decisive for the key: 'The -L option forces cd to follow symbolic links by resolving the link after processing instances of .. in dir. If .. appears in dir, cd processes it by removing the immediately previous pathname component from dir ... If neither -L nor -P is supplied, cd behaves as if -L had been supplied.' That is textual stripping of `$PWD`, by default — exactly the key. o3 is false as an option and its `why` is correct: path_resolution(7) restricts the self-referential `..` case to the actual filesystem root. o4 is directly contradicted by the same bash(1) passage. Key correct, no second defensible answer, and the FHS citation — which supported nothing in this concept — was dropped.

items.stem: An operator runs `cd '~'`, intending to go to their home directory, and instead gets "No such file or directory". What went wrong?

options.text: Quoting the tilde suppressed expansion, so the shell looked for a directory literally named `~`
options.why: Tilde expansion happens only when the tilde is unquoted and starts a word; single quotes make it a literal character like any other.

options.text: `cd` never accepts `~` as an argument, because the builtin requires either an absolute path or a plain directory name
options.why: bash(1) documents unquoted `cd ~` as a normal way to reach the home directory, and `cd` accepts relative pathnames as well; the failure here is caused specifically by the quoting.

options.text: The account's `$HOME` variable was never set, so expansion had nothing to substitute
options.why: An unset `$HOME` would also break the unquoted form; the scenario's failure is produced by the quotes, which suppress expansion regardless of `$HOME`.

options.text: The home directory does not exist on this system, independent of quoting
options.why: Nothing in the scenario indicates a missing home directory; the described symptom is the classic result of quoting a tilde.

items.rationale: Tilde expansion happens only when the tilde is unquoted and starts a word. `'~'` and `"~"` are both literal, so `cd '~'` tries to enter a directory actually named `~` rather than the account's home directory.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. o2 was self-refuting, ending 'though that is not what actually happens in practice'. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o2 rewritten as a concrete false constraint on `cd`'s argument. Key checked against bash(1) Tilde Expansion: 'If a word begins with an unquoted tilde character ("~"), all of the characters preceding the first unquoted slash ... are considered a tilde-prefix. If none of the characters in the tilde-prefix are quoted, the characters ... are treated as a possible login name. If this login name is the null string, the tilde is replaced with the value of the shell parameter HOME.' Single quotes make the tilde quoted, so no expansion occurs and `cd` is handed the literal name `~`. o3 is false: bash(1) adds 'If HOME is unset, the tilde expands to the home directory of the user executing the shell instead', so an unset `$HOME` would not even break the unquoted form the way the option claims — the `why` was rewritten in an earlier wave and is correct that quoting alone produces this failure. o4 is ruled out by the scenario. Key correct, no second defensible answer.

items.stem: A colleague insists a directory holds several configuration files, but plain `ls` on that directory prints nothing at all. What is the most likely explanation, and how would you confirm it?

options.text: The files are dotfiles; `ls -la` would reveal them along with `.` and `..`
options.why: `ls` omits any name starting with a dot by default, so a directory holding only dotfiles looks empty under a plain listing even though it is not.

options.text: The directory has been corrupted and needs `fsck` before it can be listed
options.why: A truly corrupted directory produces a filesystem error, not a clean, silent empty listing; the scenario matches ordinary dotfile hiding instead.

options.text: The colleague is looking at a different host, so the discrepancy is expected
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests two hosts are involved; the question is asking for the local, technical explanation for an empty-looking listing.

options.text: Plain `ls` requires `-l` before it will print any entries at all
options.why: Plain `ls` prints names without `-l`; the long-format flag changes how much detail is shown, not whether entries appear.

options.why: `pwd` prints the full pathname of the current working directory — precisely the value a relative path would be resolved against.

items.stem: An instruction says to "change to root's home directory." A junior operator runs `cd /home/root` and gets "No such file or directory." Comparing the root directory, `/root`, and a regular user's home shows why the instruction was misread. Where should they actually go, and why does `/home/root` not exist?

options.why: `cd` reports permission errors directly when it cannot enter a directory it can otherwise see; no other command is involved here.

items.stem: A deployment script needs to create `/srv/app/logs/2026` in one step, even when `/srv/app/logs` does not exist yet, and must not fail if the full path already exists from a previous run. Which command satisfies both requirements?

options.why: `-p` creates every missing parent and, uniquely among these options, does not fail if the directory already exists, which is what makes it safe to rerun.

options.why: Without `-p`, `mkdir` fails with "No such file or directory" the moment an intermediate parent is missing, and it also errors on a directory that already exists.

options.text: Running `touch /srv/app/logs/2026` to bring the path into existence
options.why: `touch` creates or updates a file's timestamps; it does not create directories at all.

options.text: Running `cp -r /srv/app/logs /srv/app/logs/2026` to duplicate the parent tree
options.why: Copying a directory tree is unrelated to creating a new, empty nested directory, and would require the source to already exist.

items.stem: An operator wants to remove a directory only if it is completely empty, and to be told about it if it is not, rather than having the contents silently swept away. Which command gives that behaviour?

options.text: Running `rmdir` against the target directory, refusing outright if anything remains inside
options.why: `rmdir` deliberately refuses and reports an error on any directory that still has contents, which is a safety feature rather than a limitation.

options.text: Running `rm -r`, which recurses through the tree and clears everything it finds
options.why: `rm -r` recurses into a directory and deletes everything inside it without stopping to check whether it was empty.

options.text: Running `rm -i` and confirming each file individually as it goes
options.why: Prompting per file still allows the deletion to proceed once confirmed; it does not refuse based on the directory being non-empty the way `rmdir` does.

items.stem: A script runs `rm -rf "$DIR/"` at a stage where `$DIR` turns out to be unset. What single operand does the shell hand to `rm`?

options.text: `/`, because the empty expansion leaves only the trailing slash behind
options.why: An unset variable inside double quotes expands to the empty string, so the word collapses to `/`. GNU `rm` happens to refuse that one path — `--preserve-root` is its default — but the protection covers `/` alone, so the same bug with `$DIR` set to a wrong value gets none of it.

options.why: The trailing slash in `"$DIR/"` survives the expansion of the empty variable, leaving a real operand rather than none.

options.text: The literal text `$DIR/`, since the shell leaves an unset variable's name in place
options.why: Parameter expansion runs whether or not the variable is set; an unset variable expands to the empty string, not to its own name.

options.text: `.`, since the shell substitutes the current directory for a missing path segment
options.why: There is no such substitution; the shell performs no fallback to `.` when a variable is empty — it simply expands to nothing.

items.stem: An operator needs to page back and forth through a multi-gigabyte log file without flooding the terminal and without waiting for the whole file to load first. Which tool is designed for that, and why does it start instantly?

options.text: `less`, because it reads lazily and only loads what it currently displays
options.why: less(1) states that it 'does not have to read the entire input file before starting, so with large input files it starts up faster than text editors like vi', and it allows backward as well as forward movement through the file.

options.text: `cat`, because concatenating the file to standard output is the fastest way to read it
options.why: `cat` dumps the entire file to standard output at once, which floods the terminal on a multi-gigabyte log rather than paging through it.

options.text: `head`, because showing only the first lines avoids reading the rest of the file
options.why: `head` prints only the first part of a file and exits, so it gives a quick look but never lets the operator move on through the rest.

options.text: `tail -f`, because following the file avoids ever loading its earlier contents
options.why: `tail -f` is for watching new lines as they are appended to a growing file, not for reading through an existing large file from the start.

items.rationale: `less` reads lazily, allowing backward movement and searching, and opens instantly on a huge file because it only loads what it displays — unlike `cat`, which dumps the whole file to standard output at once.

items.stem: A log file is rotated at midnight, and a `tail -f` window watching it goes permanently silent afterward even though new entries are clearly being written. Which option fixes this, and why did plain `-f` fail?

options.text: `tail -F`, because it follows the file by name and reopens after rotation
options.why: `-f` follows the open file descriptor, so after rotation it keeps watching the old, now-unwritten file; `-F` follows the name instead and reopens the new file that takes its place.

options.text: `tail -n 20`, because increasing the starting line count restores visibility

options.text: `head -c`, because reading by byte count survives rotation where line following does not
options.why: `head` reads from the beginning of a file and does not follow growth at all, so it cannot be the fix for a stalled follow.

options.why: `tail -F` specifically exists to solve this exact problem by reopening the file after rotation, so the situation is not unfixable.

items.stem: A file was created thirty seconds ago and must be located immediately by name across a large tree. Comparing the tools that answer "where is this file," which one should be used, and which should be ruled out?

options.text: `find`, because it walks the tree live; `locate` would miss a file this recent
options.why: `find` inspects the filesystem as it walks it, while `locate` queries a database refreshed periodically by `updatedb` and would not yet know about a thirty-second-old file.

options.text: `locate`, because it is faster and speed is what the scenario asks for
options.why: Speed is real, but `locate` trades it for freshness: its index is only as current as the last `updatedb` run, which a thirty-second-old file has certainly missed.

options.text: `which`, because it searches every directory a file could have been created in
options.why: which(1) prints the full path of the executable that would run for a command name, searching only the directories listed in `PATH`; it has nothing to do with locating an arbitrary file by name.

options.text: `whereis`, because it searches the whole filesystem for any name given to it — it walks every mounted filesystem before reporting
options.why: whereis(1) 'locates the binary, source and manual files for the specified command names' by looking in standard Linux places and the directories named by `$PATH` and `$MANPATH`, not by walking the filesystem for an arbitrary name.

items.rationale: `find` walks a directory tree live and filters on name, type, size, timestamp or permission, so it always sees a file the moment it exists. `locate` queries a prebuilt index and is faster but can be stale, which rules it out for a file created moments ago.

items.stem: An operator runs `find . -name *.log` in a directory whose only `.log` file is `error.log`, and the results contain nothing but files named `error.log`, even though several other `.log` files exist in subdirectories. What went wrong with the command?

items.stem: An operator wants to know exactly which file on `PATH` will run when they type `git`, in case more than one copy is installed. Which command answers that directly?

options.text: `which -a git`, showing every matching file on `PATH`, not just the first
options.why: which(1) prints the full path of the executable that would have run for the name given, searching `PATH` with the same algorithm as the shell, and '--all, -a  Print all matching executables in PATH, not just the first.'

options.text: `whereis git`, since it reports the binary's location along with its manual page and source paths
options.why: `whereis` looks only in a compiled-in list of standard directories, which may miss a copy installed elsewhere on `PATH`, unlike `which`'s actual `PATH` lookup.

options.text: `locate git`, since the database includes every file on the system
options.why: `locate` searches a filename index for anything matching "git" anywhere on the filesystem, which is a much broader and less precise answer than "which file on `PATH` runs."

options.why: That finds files named `git` anywhere on the filesystem, including ones nowhere near `PATH`, rather than answering which one the shell would actually execute.

items.stem: A file is named `report.txt`, but something about opening it as plain text fails. Which command determines what the file actually is, based on its content rather than its name?

options.text: `file`, which inspects the content and reports the real type
options.why: file(1) 'tests each argument in an attempt to classify it. There are three sets of tests, performed in this order: filesystem tests, magic tests, and language tests' — all against the actual bytes, so it is right even when the extension is misleading.

items.stem: An investigator runs `stat` on a file and reads its `ctime` as "when this file was created." Why is that reading wrong?

options.text: `ctime` is the inode's status-change time, which is not a creation timestamp at all
options.why: stat(1) documents `%z` as the 'time of last status change': it moves whenever the inode changes — ownership, permissions, link count — even if the contents did not. Where a filesystem records a creation time at all, `stat` reports it as a separate field, `%w`.

options.text: `ctime` is correct for creation, but only on filesystems that support it
options.why: `ctime` never records creation on any filesystem; where a birth time exists, `stat` exposes it separately as `%w`, not as `ctime`.

options.text: `atime` is the field that should have been read instead, since it tracks the earliest access
options.why: `atime` records the most recent read, not the earliest one, and is not a creation timestamp either.

options.text: `stat` reports creation time correctly, and the confusion is with `mtime` instead
options.why: `mtime` is `%y`, the time of last data modification — another non-creation timestamp; none of `atime`, `mtime` or `ctime` records when a file came into existence.

items.rationale: `ctime` is the last change to the inode itself, including a permission or ownership change, not a creation time. Traditional Unix metadata simply has no field recording when a file was originally created.

items.stem: An `ls -l` listing shows a file's timestamp column, and an operator wants that same value to be the file's access time rather than its default meaning. Which option produces that?

options.text: `ls -lu`, which shows `atime` in place of the default `mtime`
options.why: `ls -l` shows `mtime` by default, and `-u` switches the displayed timestamp to `atime`, the last read time.

options.text: `ls -lc`, which shows `atime` because `c` stands for "current access"
options.why: `ls -lc` shows `ctime`, the inode change time, not `atime`; the mnemonic in the option name does not match what the flag actually selects.

options.text: Plain `ls -l`, since the timestamp column already defaults to access time
options.why: `ls -l` shows `mtime` — the last content modification — by default, not `atime`.

options.text: `stat -f`, since it reports on the filesystem rather than an individual file
options.why: GNU `stat -f` switches to reporting on the filesystem itself, an unrelated mode that does not produce a per-file access-time listing.

items.rationale: `ls -l` shows `mtime` by default; `ls -lc` shows `ctime` and `ls -lu` shows `atime`. The three timestamps are `atime` (last read), `mtime` (last content change) and `ctime` (last inode change).

items.stem: A symlink points at a large file, and an operator wants a copy of the symlink itself — a small file pointing at the same target — rather than a full copy of the target's contents. Plain `cp` does not give that. Which option does?

options.text: `cp -a`, which preserves symlinks instead of following them
options.why: Plain `cp` follows a symbolic link and copies the target's contents; `cp -a` is archive mode, documented as `-dR --preserve=all`, and the `-d` part is `--no-dereference`, so the link itself is copied along with mode, ownership and timestamps.

options.text: `cp -L`, since dereferencing is what tells `cp` to copy the link entry itself
options.why: `-L` is `--dereference`, documented as "always follow symbolic links in SOURCE", so it produces a full copy of the target's contents, which is the opposite of what is wanted.

options.text: `ln -s` run against the copy after the fact, to convert it back into a link
options.why: By that point the full target contents have already been copied; recreating a symlink afterward does not undo the unwanted full copy.

options.text: `mv` instead of `cp`, since moving preserves everything by definition
options.why: `mv` relocates the symlink rather than copying it, which is a different operation entirely and does not answer "how do I copy a symlink as a symlink."

items.rationale: Plain `cp` follows a symbolic link and copies the target's contents, and so do `cp -L` and `cp -p`. Archive mode `cp -a` expands to `-dR --preserve=all`, and its `-d` (`--no-dereference`) component is what preserves the link itself; `cp -d`, `cp -P` and recursive `cp -r` preserve links for the same reason. The same family also covers `ls -la` for a full listing, `stat` and `file` for inspecting an entry, `mv` for relocation, `ln -s` for creating a link, and `rm -i` for a confirmed removal.

items.stem: An operator runs `ln -s config.yaml /etc/app/current.yaml` while standing in `/home/ops`, expecting the link to point at `/home/ops/config.yaml`. Where does the link actually resolve, and why?

options.text: To `/etc/app/config.yaml`, because a relative target is resolved from the link's own directory
options.why: `ln -s` records exactly the text it is given, and a relative target is resolved relative to the directory the *link* lives in, not the directory the operator was standing in when they created it.

options.text: To `/home/ops/config.yaml`, because the target is always resolved from the working directory at creation time
options.why: That is precisely the assumption the guide warns against; the target is resolved relative to the link's own directory, not the creator's working directory.

options.text: The link creation fails outright, since `config.yaml` is not an absolute path
options.why: `ln -s` accepts a relative target without complaint; it simply records the text and resolves it later relative to the link's location, which can silently produce an unintended path.

options.text: To whichever `config.yaml` is found first on `PATH`
options.why: `PATH` lookup applies to locating executable commands, not to resolving a symlink's stored target text.

items.rationale: `ln -s` records exactly the text it is given as the link's target. A relative target is resolved relative to the link's own directory, not the directory the operator was standing in when they ran the command, so `ln -s config.yaml /etc/app/current.yaml` points at `/etc/app/config.yaml`.

items.stem: Two directory entries, `report.txt` and `report-copy.txt`, both point at the same inode as a hard link pair. One of them is deleted. What happens to the data, and to the link count reported by `ls -l`?

options.text: The data stays reachable through the remaining name, and the link count drops by one
options.why: A hard link is an additional directory entry pointing at the same inode; there is no "original," so deleting one name leaves the data reachable through the other while the link count in `ls -l`'s second column falls by one.

options.text: The data is lost immediately, since deleting either hard-linked name removes the underlying file
options.why: A hard link has no primary or original entry; the inode and its data persist as long as any directory entry still references it.

options.text: The remaining name becomes a dangling reference, the same as a broken symbolic link
options.why: Dangling references are a symbolic-link failure mode, where the link is a separate file holding a path; a hard link has no such concept because it is a second name for the same inode.

options.text: The link count is unaffected, since `ls -l` only counts subdirectories, not hard links
options.why: For a regular file, the link count in `ls -l`'s second column is exactly the number of hard-linked names; it does change when one is removed.

items.rationale: A hard link is an additional directory entry pointing at the same inode, with no "original." Deleting either name leaves the data reachable through the other, and the link count `ls -l` shows drops by one.

verification.reasoning: Key verified against unlink(2): "unlink() deletes a name from the filesystem. If that name was the last link to a file and no processes have the file open, the file is deleted" — so with two hard links, removing one leaves the data reachable through the other. The link-count column is settled by POSIX ls, whose -l record format is "%s %u %s %s %u %s %s", <file mode>, <number of links>, <owner name>, <group name>, <size>, <date and time>, <pathname>, putting the number of links in the second field as the item states. Distractors: o2 (data lost immediately) contradicts unlink(2)'s last-link condition; o3 (dangling reference) describes a symbolic-link failure mode, and unlink(2) treats a symlink as its own separate case ("If the name referred to a symbolic link, the link is removed"); o4 claims the second column counts only subdirectories, which POSIX ls contradicts by defining it as the number of links for every file type. Each why states a true fact. Citation moved off gnu-coreutils-manual (unreachable) to unlink(2) and POSIX ls.

items.stem: A long listing shows `drwxr-xr-x` for a directory. Who, specifically, is permitted to create a new file inside it?

options.text: Only the owner, since only the owner triad includes `w`
options.why: On a directory, `w` is what allows creating, deleting or renaming entries inside it, and in `drwxr-xr-x` only the first (owner) triad has `w` set.

options.text: The owner and the group, since both triads include `r` and `x`
options.why: Read and execute on a directory govern listing and traversal, not creation; creating an entry specifically requires `w`, which only the owner triad has here.

options.text: Everyone, since `x` is set for owner, group and other alike
options.why: `x` on a directory permits traversal — resolving a path through it — not creating new entries, which needs `w` specifically.

options.text: No one, since `w` does not appear anywhere in `drwxr-xr-x`
options.why: Reading `rwxr-xr-x` triad by triad, the owner's triad is `rwx`, which does include `w`; only group and other lack it here.

items.rationale: On a directory, `r` means list the names inside, `x` means traverse it, and `w` means create, delete or rename entries inside it. In `drwxr-xr-x`, only the owner triad (`rwx`) has `w` set, so only the owner may create a file there.

verification.reasoning: Key verified against chmod(1) — "The letters rwxXst select file mode bits for the affected users: read (r), write (w), execute (or search for directories) (x)" — and against unlink(2), whose EACCES is "Write access to the directory containing path is not allowed", i.e. creating and removing entries in a directory is governed by that directory's w bit. path_resolution(7) confirms the triad reading: "Of the three bits used, the first bit determines read permission, the second write permission, and the last execute permission in case of ordinary files, or search permission in case of directories." In drwxr-xr-x only the owner triad carries w, so only the owner may create an entry. Distractors: o2 says r and x suffice, contradicted by the search-permission sentence above; o3 says x alone allows creation, same contradiction; o4 claims no triad has w, which is false on inspection of rwxr-xr-x. Whys all state true facts and no two options agree. Citation moved off gnu-coreutils-manual (unreachable) to chmod(1), path_resolution(7) and unlink(2), which carry the sentences.

items.stem: Convert the mode string `-rw-r--r--` to its octal equivalent, and state what kind of entry it describes.

options.text: 644, a regular file the owner can read and write and everyone else can only read
options.why: Each triad is one octal digit — `r`=4, `w`=2, `x`=1 — so `rw-` is 6, `r--` is 4 twice, giving 644; the leading `-` marks a regular file, not a directory.

options.text: 755, a directory the owner can fully control and others can list and traverse
options.why: 755 corresponds to `rwxr-xr-x`, which includes execute bits this mode string does not have, and the leading `-` marks a regular file, not a directory.

options.text: 600, a private file only its owner can read or write
options.why: 600 corresponds to `rw-------`, with no access at all for group or other; this mode string grants read to both, which 600 does not.

options.text: 444, a file that is read-only for every class, since none of the three triads carries a write bit
options.why: 444 corresponds to `r--r--r--`, and it is true that it grants no write anywhere; the mode string here is `-rw-r--r--`, whose owner triad is `rw-` and does include write, so 644 is the value.

items.rationale: Each permission triad is one octal digit, with `r`=4, `w`=2 and `x`=1 added together. `-rw-r--r--` is owner `rw-` (6), group `r--` (4), other `r--` (4), giving 644 — a regular file the owner can read and write and everyone else can only read.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. Content was right but o4 was a self-refuting distractor: its text ended "...treating the two trailing `r--` triads as if they defined the whole permission set including the owner's", a trailing clause that names the misreading and so tells the reader the option is the wrong one before they reason about it. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o4 rewritten to assert the false claim plainly ("none of the three triads carries a write bit") with the correction moved into its why, keeping its length in line with the other distractors so no length cue opens. Key re-verified against chmod(1): "A numeric mode is from one to four octal digits (0-7), derived by adding up the bits with values 4, 2, and 1 ... The second digit selects permissions for the user who owns the file: read (4), write (2), and execute (1); the third selects permissions for other users in the file's group ... and the fourth for other users not in the file's group" — rw- = 6, r-- = 4, r-- = 4, so 644. The leading `-` is settled by POSIX ls's entry-type table, where `-` is "Regular file" and `d` is "Directory". o2 (755) and o3 (600) re-checked: both name modes with different bit patterns than `-rw-r--r--`, and their whys state that correctly. Citation moved off gnu-coreutils-manual (unreachable) to chmod(1) and POSIX ls.

items.stem: An operator runs `ls -l /etc/nginx` to check that directory's own permissions, but the output lists the files inside it instead. Which command replaces the listing of contents with a single line for the directory entry itself?

options.text: Running `ls -ld /etc/nginx` to target the directory entry itself
options.why: `-d` operates on the directory entry itself rather than listing its contents, which is exactly what plain `ls -l` on a directory path does not do.

options.text: `ls -lR /etc/nginx`, since a recursive listing opens with a line describing the directory itself
options.why: A recursive listing prints the directory's path as a plain header followed by its contents, then repeats that for each subdirectory; no mode string for `/etc/nginx` itself appears in that output.

options.text: `stat -d /etc/nginx`, since `-d` means "directory mode" for `stat` as well
options.why: `stat` has no `-d` option with that meaning, and borrowing another command's flag letter is a guess rather than a reading of `stat`'s own option list.

options.text: `ls -l /etc/nginx/.`, since appending a dot forces the directory's own entry to show
options.why: A trailing `.` still names the directory's contents as the thing to list, producing the same result as omitting it, not the directory's own line.

items.rationale: `ls -l` on a directory path lists the contents rather than the directory itself; only `ls -ld` shows the directory's own mode, combining `-d` (operate on the directory itself) with `-l`.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. Against the original stem ("Which command shows the directory's own mode string?") that option was defensible, which is the two-correct-answers defect. Key verified against ls(1): "-d, --directory: list directories themselves, not their contents". o3 re-read: `stat` has no such `-d`; its why was reworded to drop a reference to what "the exam probes" and to state the plain fact instead. o4 (`ls -l /etc/nginx/.`) re-checked: a trailing `.` still names the directory whose contents are listed, so the output is unchanged; POSIX ls confirms that without -d a directory operand causes its contents to be written. items.stem: An application running as user `svc` gets "Permission denied" opening `/srv/app/data/config.yaml`, which is mode 644 and owned by `svc`. Working outward from the file, what should be checked next, and why might the file's own mode be irrelevant to the failure?

options.text: The execute bit on every directory in the path, since a missing `x` on any parent blocks traversal regardless of the file's own mode
options.why: On a directory, `x` governs whether a path can be traversed through it to reach a named entry; a file with mode 644 in a directory that lacks `x` for `svc` is unreachable no matter what its own permissions say.

options.text: Whether the file has been renamed, since a rename would explain a permission error
options.why: A renamed or missing file produces "No such file or directory," not "Permission denied," so a rename does not match the error described.

options.text: The group ownership only, since 644 already grants the owner full access
options.why: Exactly one triad applies to a given access attempt, and since `svc` owns the file the owner triad — which already grants read — is the one that decides; group ownership is irrelevant here.

options.text: Whether the filesystem is mounted read-only, since a read-only mount refuses to open any file on it
options.why: A read-only mount blocks writes, and an attempt to write there fails with "Read-only file system" rather than "Permission denied"; opening a file for reading on such a mount still succeeds.

items.rationale: For a "permission denied" on a path, the diagnostic order works outward: first decide which triad applies (here, owner, which 644 already permits), then check the execute bit on every directory in the path — a file with a permissive mode in a directory that blocks traversal is still unreachable.

Key verified against path_resolution(7): "If the process does not have search permission on the current lookup directory, an EACCES error is returned (\"Permission denied\")", and "the last execute permission in case of ordinary files, or search permission in case of directories" — so a missing x on any parent directory blocks the open regardless of the file's own 644 mode. o2 re-checked against the same page: a missing component yields ENOENT, "No such file or directory", not "Permission denied", so its why is true. o3 re-checked: path_resolution(7) states the owner triad is the one applied when the process's effective UID matches the file owner, so group ownership is indeed irrelevant here. chmod(1) supplies the r/w/x letter meanings. Citation moved off gnu-coreutils-manual (unreachable).

items.stem: A mode string begins with the letter `l` rather than `-` or `d`. What kind of filesystem entry does that indicate?

options.text: A symbolic link
options.why: The leading type character is `l` specifically for a symbolic link, distinct from `-` for a regular file and `d` for a directory.

options.text: A regular file with the immutable attribute set
options.why: File attributes such as immutability are not represented in the leading type character at all; a regular file always shows `-` there regardless of its attributes.

options.text: A directory that has reached its link-count limit
options.why: Link-count limits are not represented in the type character either, and a directory always shows `d` there, not `l`.

options.text: A hard link, as opposed to an ordinary file
options.why: A hard link is simply an additional name for an ordinary inode and shows the same `-` type character as any other regular file; `l` is reserved for symbolic links.

So a leading `l` is a symbolic link and nothing else. items.stem: A repository built on macOS, whose default filesystem is case-insensitive but case-preserving, is extracted on a Linux server running ext4. It contained both `Readme.md` and `readme.md`, which macOS treated as one file. What happens on the Linux server?

items.rationale: `export NAME=value` assigns and exports in one step, and `export` may also be applied after a plain assignment; either way, what matters is that the variable has been exported before the child process that needs it starts.
