items.stem: Comparing `set` with no arguments against `env`, what is the difference in what each lists, and how does that explain a variable that appears in one but not the other?

options.text: `set` lists all shell variables and functions; `env` lists only exported ones
options.why: A variable visible in `set` but absent from `env` is exactly a shell variable that was assigned but never exported, so it has never left the current shell.

options.text: `set` lists only exported variables, and `env` lists everything including functions
options.why: This reverses the roles: `set` is the broader listing including unexported variables and functions, while `env` (and `printenv`) shows only the exported subset.

options.text: Both list identical output; any difference indicates a corrupted shell session
options.why: The two commands are expected to differ whenever unexported shell variables exist; that difference is normal, not a sign of corruption.

options.text: `env` includes variables from every user's login shell, not just the current one
options.why: `env` reports the current process's own environment, not other users' sessions; it is scoped to the invoking shell just as `set` is.

items.rationale: `set` with no arguments lists all shell variables and functions; `env` (and `printenv`) lists only exported ones. A variable visible in `set` but absent from `env` is exactly a shell variable that was never exported.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED for its sourcing: the item compares `set` against `env`, and cited posix-shell-command-language, which describes neither utility's no-argument output (`set` and `env` have their own utility pages, and `env` is not part of the shell command language at all). REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: env(1) now carries the `env` half and bash(1) the `set` half. Key verified from both sides. bash(1)'s set builtin: "Without options, display the name and value of each shell variable in a format that can be reused as input for setting or resetting the currently-set variables ... In posix mode, only shell variables are listed" — the posix-mode caveat is what establishes that ordinary bash also lists function definitions, so the key's "all shell variables and functions" holds for the default interactive shell the item describes. env(1): "If no COMMAND, print the resulting environment", and the environment is by definition the exported set (bash(1) export: names "marked for automatic export to the environment"). A variable in set but not env is therefore an unexported shell variable. Distractors: o2 reverses the two roles, refuted by both sentences; o3 says identical output signals corruption, refuted because unexported variables are ordinary; o4 claims env spans other users' login shells, refuted by env(1) describing the current invocation's own environment. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1) and env(1).

items.stem: A line containing `!!` behaves as expected when typed at an interactive prompt, but the identical line inside a script does nothing of the kind. Why does the same syntax behave differently in the two contexts?

options.text: History expansion is disabled in non-interactive shells, so `!!` in a script is not treated specially
options.why: History expansion is an interactive-only feature; a script containing `!!` does not get the previous-command substitution the same text produces at a live prompt.

options.text: Scripts silently rewrite `!!` into the literal text of the last command run interactively
options.why: A script has no access to the interactive shell's history at all; it simply does not perform history expansion, rather than substituting anything from a separate session.

options.text: `!!` is bash-only syntax that fails the same way at a prompt and in a script, since no shell has ever implemented it
options.why: The scenario states `!!` behaves as expected at the interactive prompt, so it is not uniformly broken; bash documents `!` style history substitution and enables it by default for interactive shells.

options.text: The script needs `source` instead of direct execution for history expansion to apply
options.why: Sourcing runs a script in the current shell but does not itself enable history expansion, which is governed by interactive-versus-non-interactive mode, not by how the script is invoked.

items.rationale: History expansion is an interactive-shell feature. `!!` is replaced by the previous command line at a live prompt, but a script containing the same characters runs in a non-interactive shell, where history expansion is off.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. o3's text ended "since the scenario is read as a portability problem rather than an interactive-versus-script distinction", which describes the reader's error instead of making a claim, marking the option as wrong before it is evaluated. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o3 now states a flatly false claim and its why carries the refutation. Key verified against bash(1)'s set builtin option list: "-H Enable ! style history substitution. This option is on by default when the shell is interactive" — so a non-interactive shell running a script does not perform history expansion at all. o2 (a script rewrites `!!` from the interactive session's history) is refuted because a script's shell has its own history state and, per the same option, no expansion enabled; o4 (`source` would enable it) is refuted because -H tracks interactivity, not the method of invocation, and its why says exactly that. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1).

items.stem: An operator wants to find a long `rsync` command they typed twenty minutes ago without scrolling back through everything since. Which interactive feature is designed for exactly this?

options.text: `Ctrl-R`, which starts a reverse incremental search through history
options.why: Pressing `Ctrl-R` and typing part of the remembered command narrows the search as you type, and pressing it again steps to the next older match.

options.text: `history`, which always jumps straight to the most relevant past command automatically
options.why: `history` lists the numbered command history for the operator to read through; it does not search or jump to a specific past command on its own.

options.text: Tab completion, since it recalls whole previous commands the same way it completes filenames
options.why: Tab completion fills in a partly typed name from what exists on disk or in known commands; it does not search backward through command history.

options.text: `!$`, since it reruns whichever command last used the word "rsync"
options.why: `!$` reuses the previous command line's last argument, not a search by keyword across history; it has no notion of finding a specific past command by content.

items.rationale: `Ctrl-R` starts a reverse incremental search through the history list: typing narrows the match, pressing it again steps to the next older one, which is exactly the tool for finding a specific past command without scrolling.

verification.reasoning: Key verified against bash(1)'s readline command list: "reverse-search-history (C-r): Search backward starting at the current line and moving 'up' through the history as necessary. This is an incremental search" — an incremental backward search by content, which is what the operator needs. Distractors: o2 claims `history` jumps to the most relevant past command, but bash(1) documents the history builtin as displaying the history list with line numbers, with no search-and-jump behaviour; o3 claims tab completion recalls whole previous commands, refuted by bash(1)'s Completing section, which completes words against filenames, commands, variables and the like rather than history lines; o4 claims `!$` finds a command by keyword, refuted by bash(1)'s Word Designators, where `$` is "The last word" of the referenced line. Each why states a true fact. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1).

items.stem: A second terminal opened at the same time as a first does not show any of the first terminal's commands in its history, even though both belong to the same user. Why not?

options.text: The history file is normally written when a session ends, so a still-open first session has not written its lines yet
options.why: The shell keeps the history list in memory during a session and writes it to `HISTFILE` — `~/.bash_history` by default — typically at session exit, so a concurrently open second terminal has nothing new to read yet.

options.text: Each terminal window is permanently assigned its own separate `HISTFILE`
options.why: By default all sessions for a user share the same `HISTFILE`; the gap here is about when each session writes to it, not separate files per window.

options.text: History sharing requires tab completion to be enabled in both sessions
options.why: Tab completion and history are separate readline features; enabling one has no bearing on whether one session's commands appear in another's history.

options.text: Only commands run through `sudo` are written to the shared history file, and everything else is discarded at exit
options.why: Bash copies the session's history entries to the history file without regard to privilege; nothing in its history handling singles out `sudo` or drops unprivileged commands.

items.rationale: The shell keeps its history list in memory and writes it to `HISTFILE` — `~/.bash_history` by default — when the session ends, which is why a second terminal opened at the same time does not see the first session's commands until it exits.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. o4's text ended "since privileged commands are assumed to be logged separately from ordinary ones", a trailing clause of the 'is assumed to' form that labels the option as a misconception rather than asserting it. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o4 now makes the claim plainly, with the correction in its why. Key verified against bash(1): "When a shell with history enabled exits, bash copies the last $HISTSIZE entries from the history list to $HISTFILE. If the histappend shell option is enabled ... bash appends the entries to the history file, otherwise it overwrites the history file" — so a still-open first session has not written its lines, and a second session that read the file at startup sees nothing new. o2 (a separate HISTFILE per window) is refuted by "HISTFILE ... Bash assigns a default value of ~/.bash_history", one default path per user; o3 (history sharing requires tab completion) is refuted by the two being unrelated readline and history features. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1).

items.stem: A command that works fine when typed at the prompt fails with "command not found" when the exact same line is placed inside a script. The command turns out to be an alias. Why does it fail only in the script?

options.text: A script does not inherit aliases, because it runs in a non-interactive shell
options.why: Bash does not expand aliases in a non-interactive shell unless `expand_aliases` is explicitly set, so a name that only exists as an alias in the interactive shell is simply not found inside a script.

options.text: Aliases are copied into scripts automatically, so the failure must be a typo instead
options.why: Aliases are not automatically available to a script; that is precisely the mechanism causing the failure, not a separate typo.

options.text: The script needs `export` applied to the alias before it can be used
options.why: Aliases cannot be exported the way variables can; there is no export mechanism that makes an alias visible to a non-interactive shell.

options.text: Aliases only work when defined inside the script file itself, never in `~/.bashrc`
options.why: An alias can be defined in `~/.bashrc` and used freely at an interactive prompt; the issue is specifically that a non-interactive script does not expand aliases at all by default.

items.rationale: A script runs in a non-interactive shell, and bash does not expand aliases there unless `expand_aliases` is set with `shopt`. A name that exists only as an alias in the interactive shell is therefore not found when the same line runs inside a script. `alias` itself, run with no arguments, lists every alias currently defined.

verification.reasoning: Key verified verbatim against bash(1), ALIASES: "Aliases are not expanded when the shell is not interactive, unless the expand_aliases shell option is set using shopt", and the shopt entry confirms "expand_aliases: If set, aliases are expanded as described above under ALIASES. This option is enabled by default for interactive shells." A name that exists only as an alias therefore fails inside a script with command not found, exactly as the key says. Distractors: o2 (aliases copied into scripts automatically) is refuted by that first sentence; o3 (export the alias) is refuted by bash(1)'s export builtin, whose names are variables or, with -f, functions, with no alias form anywhere in the builtin; o4 (aliases only work when defined in the script file) is refuted by ~/.bashrc being read for interactive shells, where the alias does work. Each why states a true fact. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (www.gnu.org unreachable here) to bash(1).

items.stem: One account has `rm` aliased to `rm -i` in its `~/.bashrc`; a server account does not. The same typed `rm somefile` command behaves differently on each. Which command reveals that an alias, rather than the plain binary, is actually running?

options.text: `type rm`, which distinguishes an alias from a function, a builtin, or a file on `PATH`
options.why: `type` reports what a name actually resolves to — alias, function, builtin or file — while `which` only reports a file on `PATH` and says nothing about an alias shadowing it.

options.text: `which rm`, since it reports the exact command that will execute, the same way it reports any other name found on `PATH`
options.why: `which rm` reports the file on `PATH`, ignoring an alias entirely; it would show the same result on both accounts even though their actual behaviour differs.

options.text: `man rm`, since the man page documents any locally defined aliases
options.why: A man page documents the command itself, not a particular account's shell configuration; it has no way to reflect an alias defined in `~/.bashrc`.

options.text: `history | grep rm`, since a past invocation would reveal the alias definition
options.why: History records commands that were run, not their definitions; it does not show whether a name is currently aliased.

items.rationale: `type` distinguishes an alias from a function, a builtin and a file on `PATH`, while `which` cannot see the first three at all — it only reports the file `rm` would resolve to if there were no alias shadowing it.

verification.reasoning: Key verified against bash(1)'s type builtin: "Indicate how each name would be interpreted if used as a command name ... type prints a string which is one of alias, keyword, function, builtin, or file if name is an alias, shell reserved word, function, builtin, or executable file" — so `type rm` is what distinguishes an alias from the binary. Distractors: o2 (`which`) is wrong because `which` is an external command that searches PATH and cannot see the calling shell's alias table, so it prints the same /usr/bin/rm on both accounts; o3 (`man rm`) is wrong because a manual page documents the program, not one account's shell configuration; o4 (`history | grep rm`) is wrong because the history list records lines that were typed, not what a name currently resolves to, as bash(1)'s history builtin ("display the command history list with numbers") shows. Each why states a true fact and no two options assert the same answer. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1).

items.stem: An operator defines `alias ll='ls -alF'` directly at the prompt, uses it successfully for the rest of the session, then opens a brand-new terminal the next day and finds `ll` is gone. What was missing?

options.text: The alias was never written to a startup file, so it did not persist past that one session
options.why: Aliases defined at the prompt exist only inside the shell that read them; they must be written to a startup file such as `~/.bashrc` to survive into a new shell.

options.text: Aliases automatically expire after 24 hours regardless of where they are defined
options.why: Aliases have no built-in expiry; the only thing that ends one is the shell session closing, unless it was saved to a startup file.

options.text: The new terminal was opened as a different user, which does not share aliases
options.why: Nothing in the scenario indicates a different user; the described behaviour — an alias vanishing in a brand-new session — is the ordinary consequence of never saving it.

options.text: `ll` collides with a built-in command name, and the shell silently drops any alias that would shadow a builtin
options.why: Bash has no such rule: an alias is expanded before a builtin is looked up, so an alias may shadow one, and `ll` is not a bash builtin in any case.

items.rationale: Aliases are defined in a shell startup file, conventionally `~/.bashrc`, and exist only inside the shell that read that file. Defining one at the prompt without saving it means it does not survive into a new shell session.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. o4's text ended "since the shell is assumed to reject a user-defined alias that collides with one of its own names", an 'is assumed to' clause that flags the option as a misconception instead of asserting it. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: o4 now states the false rule plainly and its why gives the two facts that refute it. Key verified against bash(1): the alias builtin defines aliases in the running shell, and startup files are what a new shell reads, since "When an interactive shell that is not a login shell is started, bash reads and executes commands from ~/.bashrc, if that file exists" — an alias typed at the prompt is in no such file, so the next day's shell never learns it. o2 (24-hour expiry) has no counterpart anywhere in bash(1)'s ALIASES section or alias builtin; o3 (different user) contradicts the scenario, which describes the same operator opening a new terminal. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1).

items.stem: A script runs a command, then a moment later checks `$?`, but has printed a status message with `echo` in between. What value does `$?` actually report at that point?

options.text: The exit status of the `echo` command itself, not the original command
options.why: `$?` is overwritten by every command that runs, including `echo`, so it must be checked immediately after the command whose status matters, before anything else runs.

options.text: The original command's status, since `echo` does not affect shell parameters
options.why: `echo` is a command like any other and sets its own exit status when it finishes, overwriting whatever `$?` held immediately before.

options.text: The logical OR of both commands' statuses
options.why: `$?` holds a single command's status, not a combination of several; there is no such OR-of-statuses behaviour in the shell.

options.text: Whatever `PIPESTATUS` recorded for the last pipeline that ran
options.why: `PIPESTATUS` is a separate array populated only after a pipeline, and nothing in the scenario involves one; `$?` simply reflects the single most recently completed command.

items.rationale: `$?` holds the status of the most recently completed foreground command. Running any other command first — including the `echo` used to report it — overwrites that value, so it must be checked immediately. Checking it manually is always `echo $?`, run immediately after the command in question.

verification.reasoning: Key verified against bash(1)'s special parameters: "? ($?) Expands to the exit status of the most recently executed command", together with the echo builtin's own documented status: "Output the args, separated by spaces, followed by a newline. The return status is 0 unless a write error occurs." `echo` is therefore a command that sets $? like any other, and after it runs the original command's status is gone. Distractors: o2 claims echo does not affect shell parameters, refuted by that return-status sentence; o3 invents a logical OR of two statuses, which appears nowhere in bash(1)'s definition of $? as a single most-recent status; o4 points at PIPESTATUS, which bash(1) defines as "An array variable ... containing a list of exit status values from the commands in the most-recently-executed foreground pipeline", a separate variable and not what $? reports. Each why states a true fact. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1).

items.stem: A script treats `grep pattern file.txt` returning a non-zero status as proof that something went wrong. `grep` exits 1 here. Is that conclusion correct?

options.text: No — `grep` returns 1 to mean "no lines matched," and reserves 2 for a real error
options.why: Non-zero does not always mean failure: `grep`'s exit status of 1 is an ordinary, expected outcome meaning the pattern was not found, distinct from status 2, which signals an actual error.

options.text: Yes — any non-zero status from any command always indicates a real failure
options.why: Several tools, `grep` among them, define non-zero values that are not errors; treating every non-zero status as failure misreads exactly this case.

options.text: No — but only because the file was empty, which always forces status 1
options.why: Status 1 from `grep` means no matching line was found, regardless of whether that is because the file is empty or simply lacks the pattern; file emptiness is not a separate special case.

options.text: Yes — `grep` is the one exception where 1 and 2 both mean the same generic failure
options.why: `grep` distinguishes the two: 1 means no match, 2 means an actual error occurred, so they are not the same outcome collapsed into one meaning.

items.rationale: `grep` returns 1 when it simply found no matching line and 2 when it hit a real error, so treating grep's 1 as a failure of the search misreads an ordinary, expected outcome.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED for its sourcing: the whole item is about grep's exit codes, and it cited the bash manual and the POSIX Shell Command Language chapter. Neither specifies grep's statuses; the shell chapter defines only the general 0/127/126/signal cases. REPAIR AND RE-VERIFICATION: Key verified against grep(1), EXIT STATUS: "Normally the exit status is 0 if a line is selected, 1 if no lines were selected, and 2 if an error occurred. However, if the -q or --quiet or --silent is used and a line is selected, the exit status is 0 even if an error occurred." So 1 means no match, an ordinary outcome, and 2 is the error code, exactly as the key and its why say. Distractors: o2 (every non-zero status is a real failure) is refuted by that same sentence; o3 (status 1 only because the file was empty) is refuted because the status turns on whether any line was selected, with no separate empty-file case in the specification; o4 (grep collapses 1 and 2 into one generic failure) is refuted by the standard three-way split. Citation corrected: this item previously cited the bash manual and POSIX shell command language, neither of which specifies grep's exit codes; grep(1) is the page that carries them, and bash(1) is retained only for $? itself.

items.stem: A process is killed by SIGKILL, signal number 9. What exit status does the shell report for it, and what is the general rule this follows?

options.text: 137, because a signal death reports 128 plus the signal number
options.why: The convention is 128+N for a command killed by signal N, so SIGKILL (9) produces 137 and SIGTERM (15) produces 143.

options.text: 9, the signal number itself, reported directly as the exit status
options.why: The raw signal number is not used directly as the exit status; the shell reports 128 plus the signal number instead, giving 137 for SIGKILL.

options.text: 126, the same status used for a command that is found but not executable
options.why: 126 specifically means the command was found but could not be executed; a signal death is a distinct case reported as 128 plus the signal number.

options.text: 1, the generic failure value used whenever a process does not exit cleanly
options.why: Status 1 is a generic tool-defined failure value; a signal death has its own specific convention of 128 plus the signal number, not the generic 1.

items.rationale: A command killed by signal N returns 128 plus N, so a process killed by SIGKILL (9) reports 137, and one killed by SIGTERM (15) reports 143. A command not found returns 127, and one found but not executable returns 126.

verification.reasoning: Key verified twice in bash(1): "The return value of a simple command is its exit status, or 128+n if the command is terminated by signal n", and in EXIT STATUS: "When a command terminates on a fatal signal N, bash uses the value of 128+N as the exit status." SIGKILL is signal 9, so 137, and SIGTERM 15 gives 143 as the why states. POSIX agrees on the shape of the rule: "if the command terminated due to the receipt of a signal, the shell shall assign it an exit status greater than 128." Distractors: o2 (the raw signal number) is refuted by the 128+N sentence; o3 (126) is refuted by bash(1)'s adjacent statuses, "If a command is not found ... 127. If a command is found but is not [executable] ... 126", which is a different case; o4 (generic 1) is refuted by the same specific convention. Each why states a true fact. Citation moved off gnu-bash-manual (unreachable) to bash(1), with POSIX kept for the portable form of the rule.

items.stem: A command's output is captured to a file with `>`, yet an error message from that same command still appears on the screen. Comparing what "output" covers against the three numbered streams, why does this happen?

options.text: Only descriptor 1 was redirected; descriptor 2 still points at the terminal
options.why: Standard output and standard error are separate descriptors — 1 and 2 — and by default both point at the terminal; redirecting one leaves the other exactly where it was.

options.text: "Output" always includes both streams, so this must indicate a shell bug
options.why: This ambiguity is the point of the design, not a bug: only the operator that explicitly names descriptor 2 moves error messages, and `>` alone does not.

options.text: The error is arriving through a pipe from a background process instead
options.why: Nothing in the scenario involves a pipe or a background process; the error is simply travelling on the untouched descriptor 2, as it always does by default.

options.text: Errors bypass redirection entirely and cannot be captured under any circumstances
options.why: Errors can be captured with an operator that names descriptor 2, such as `2>`; they are not immune to redirection, they are simply on a separate descriptor that `>` alone does not touch.

items.rationale: A program writes results to descriptor 1 and diagnostics to descriptor 2. Both default to the terminal, so they look like one stream until something is redirected — `command > file` moves only descriptor 1, leaving descriptor 2's error messages on screen.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. bash(1) REDIRECTION: "If the first character of the redirection operator is “>”, the redirection refers to the standard output (file descriptor 1)" — so a bare `>` moves descriptor 1 only, and descriptor 2 is untouched and still on the terminal. POSIX 2.7.2 says the same for the `[n]>word` form. o2 is false: the split is by design, not a bug, and bash(1) names 1 and 2 as separate descriptors throughout. o3 is false: nothing in the stem involves a pipe or a background process. o4 is false: bash(1) `[n]>word` and POSIX 2.7.2 explicitly permit a descriptor number before the operator, which is what `2>` is. No distractor is defensible; each `why` states a true fact. Citations already fit — every claim is a shell redirection claim covered by both cited sources. items.stem: Which file descriptor numbers correspond to standard input, standard output and standard error, in that order?

options.text: 0, 1 and 2
options.why: These are the three numbered descriptors every process starts with: 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output, and 2 is standard error.

options.text: 1, 2 and 3
options.why: Descriptor numbering starts at 0 for standard input, not 1; shifting the numbers by one misassigns all three streams.

options.text: 0, 2 and 1, with error coming before output
options.why: Standard output is descriptor 1 and standard error is descriptor 2; this swaps the two, which is a common but incorrect pairing.

options.text: There are no fixed numbers; they vary by which shell is running
options.why: The numbering 0, 1 and 2 is a fixed Unix convention that every shell and program relies on, not something that varies by shell.

items.stem: A command's output is piped into `grep`, and its error messages are noticed to still appear on screen rather than being searched. Why does a plain pipe not carry them along?

options.text: A pipe connects only descriptor 1 by default, so standard error is not carried into the pipeline
options.why: The pipe operator wires standard output to the next command's standard input; standard error stays attached to the terminal unless it is explicitly merged first with `2>&1 |` or `|&`.

options.text: A pipe carries both streams by default, so `grep` should already be matching against error text too
options.why: Only descriptor 1 is connected by a plain pipe; the assumption that error text is included by default is exactly the mistake the exam probes.

options.text: `grep` specifically filters out anything that looks like an error message
options.why: `grep` has no awareness of which stream text came from; it simply matches lines against a pattern on whatever standard input it is given.

items.stem: Comparing `command > out 2>&1` with `command 2>&1 > out`, which one sends both streams to the file, and which leaves errors on the terminal?

items.stem: A build log needs both standard output and standard error captured to one file, and the script must run correctly on both bash and a strict POSIX `/bin/sh`. Which redirection is the portable choice?

options.text: Writing `> build.log 2>&1`, merging descriptor 2 onto descriptor 1 after opening the file

options.why: `tee` reads standard input from a pipe, but a plain pipe still carries only descriptor 1 by default, so error output would not reach it without the same `2>&1` merging step first.

items.stem: Comparing a pipe, a redirection, and the standard streams themselves: which one joins two running processes together, which one joins a process to a file, and which one is just the numbered endpoints?

options.text: A pipe joins two processes; redirection joins a process to a file or descriptor; standard streams are the numbered endpoints 0, 1 and 2

options.why: This swaps the two roles: a pipe is what connects two running processes concurrently, and redirection is what attaches a stream to a file.

options.text: All three describe the same mechanism under different names, with the choice of word being purely a matter of habit
options.why: The three are distinct: what sits at the far end of the connection — another process, a file, or nothing yet decided — is exactly the separating axis between them.

options.text: Standard streams come into existence only once a pipe or redirection has been used; a process run with neither has no descriptors open at all
options.why: Every process starts with all three descriptors already open, attached to the terminal by default, whether or not a pipe or redirection is ever applied.

options.text: `whereis`, since it searches every standard location for matching text, the same way it searches those locations for a command's binary

items.stem: A pattern copied from documentation uses `colou?r` to match both "color" and "colour" with `grep`, but run without `-E` it finds nothing. Why?

options.why: grep interprets its pattern argument as a regular expression, not a glob; `?` there means "optional" only under extended syntax, not the glob meaning of "exactly one character".

options.text: grep requires quantifiers to be written in brackets, such as `[?]`, which is the bracket syntax that turns an ordinary character into an operator
options.why: Wrapping `?` in brackets would make it a literal character class matching a literal question mark, not enable it as a quantifier; that is not how extended syntax is requested.

items.stem: The glob `*.txt` and a regular expression both use `.` and `*`, but a pattern written for one tool copied unchanged into the other silently matches the wrong thing. What is the underlying reason for that inversion?

options.why: The two pattern languages assign different meanings to the same characters, so a pattern copied from one context to the other changes meaning without producing any error to flag it.

options.text: Regular expressions do not use `.` as a metacharacter at all; only globs assign it a special meaning, leaving it an ordinary literal dot in every regex dialect
options.why: A regular expression's `.` is one of its most common metacharacters, matching any single character; it is very much defined there.

options.text: The inversion only affects `sed`, not `grep`, since they use different regex engines entirely
options.why: Both `grep` and `sed` default to the same basic regular expression dialect, so the glob-versus-regex inversion applies to patterns used with either tool.

options.text: Only the last line of the file, matching `tail`'s default behaviour
options.why: sed processes and prints the entire input stream line by line by default; it does not restrict itself to the final line the way `tail` does.

items.stem: A task asks to print the third whitespace-separated column of a report where the columns are separated by a ragged, variable number of spaces. Comparing awk against sed for this job, which is the right tool, and why?

options.text: awk, because it splits each line into fields and a run of whitespace is its default separator
options.why: awk works on the record split into fields — `$1`, `$3`, `$NF` — and its default field separator is a run of whitespace, which is exactly why ragged columns still line up correctly.

options.text: sed, because its substitution syntax can target any column position directly
options.why: sed operates on the line as an undivided string for substitution and deletion; it has no native concept of numbered fields the way awk does.

options.why: awk and sed differ specifically on whether the unit of work is fields or the whole line, which is exactly why one fits a columnar task and the other does not.

options.text: `cut`, because it always handles variable-width columns as easily as fixed-width ones
options.why: `cut` splits on a single fixed delimiter character, so repeated spaces each count as a separate delimiter and produce empty fields on ragged columnar output.

items.rationale: awk reads input one record at a time, splits it into fields, and its default field separator is a run of whitespace with leading and trailing whitespace ignored — exactly why `awk '{print $3}'` correctly picks a column even when the spacing is ragged, which sed and `cut` cannot do as naturally. items.stem: An operator writes `awk "{print $1}" /etc/passwd` inside double quotes and gets empty output with no error. What consumed the `$1` before awk ever ran?

options.text: The shell expanded `$1` as its own positional parameter, usually empty, before awk saw the program
options.why: Double quotes still allow the shell to expand `$` expressions, so `$1` is read as the shell's own first positional parameter — typically unset — leaving awk with an empty program fragment instead of a field reference.

options.why: `$1` is valid awk field syntax; the problem here is that the shell consumed it before awk ever received the program text.

options.text: `/etc/passwd` has no first field, so `$1` legitimately prints nothing
options.why: `/etc/passwd` does have a first, colon-delimited field — the username — so a working `$1` reference would print it; the empty output is a quoting problem, not a data problem.

options.text: awk requires `-F` to be set before any field variable will be recognised
options.why: `$1` is recognised without `-F`; that flag only changes the field separator, not whether field variables are read at all.

items.rationale: Single-quoting the program is essential. Inside double quotes the shell expands `$1` first, so awk receives an empty program fragment and prints empty lines with no error to explain it.

items.stem: A colon-delimited file has some rows with consecutive colons producing empty fields, and the task is to extract the fourth field with awk using `-F:`. What happens to a run of consecutive delimiters when the separator is set to a single explicit character this way?

options.why: `uniq` compares whole lines by default and works without `cut`; the missing step here is sorting, not field extraction.

items.stem: Running `diff -u old.conf new.conf` produces a unified-format hunk with a line prefixed `-` and another prefixed `+`. Which file does the `-` line come from?

options.text: The first file, `old.conf`, which is present there and absent from `new.conf`
options.why: In unified output, the `---` header names the first file and `+++` names the second; a `-` line is present in the first file and absent from the second, while `+` marks the reverse.

options.text: The second file, `new.conf` — the operands are read right to left
options.why: The operands are read left to right, matching the order given on the command line, so `-` corresponds to the first-named file, not the second.

options.text: Neither file specifically; `-` marks a line that was moved rather than added or removed
options.why: Unified diff has no separate "moved" marker; a line simply present in one file and absent in the other shows as removed (`-`) or added (`+`).

options.why: The assignment of `-` and `+` follows the order the files were given on the command line, not alphabetical order.

items.stem: Two binary files need to be checked for whether they are byte-for-byte identical across two different machines. Comparing `diff`, `cmp`, and a checksum tool, which is the right choice, and why do the other two fall short?

options.text: A checksum tool such as `sha256sum`, since it gives a comparable fingerprint without transferring either file
options.why: `diff` on binary files only reports that they differ, with no detail; `cmp` gives the first differing byte but still requires both files on the same machine to compare directly, while a checksum can be computed independently on each host and compared.

options.text: `diff`, since its unified format applies equally well to binary and text files

options.text: `cmp`, since it can compare two files that are not both present on the same machine
options.why: `cmp` reports the first differing byte, but it needs direct access to both files at once, so it cannot compare files that are only ever present on separate machines.

options.text: Any of the three works equally well for this task, since all three reduce to the same byte-level comparison once given two files as arguments
options.why: Only a checksum tool avoids needing both files present together and gives a fingerprint suited to cross-machine comparison; the other two require direct, simultaneous access to both files.

items.rationale: For binary files, `diff` only reports that they differ; `cmp` gives the first differing byte but still needs both files locally; a checksum tool such as `sha256sum` is the right way to ask "are these two files identical" across separate machines.

items.stem: A script runs `diff a.conf b.conf && echo same` to report whether two config files match, and the message never prints even when they visibly differ, which the script treats as a bug in `diff`. Is that the right read of `diff`'s exit status here?

options.why: `diff` reserves 0 specifically for identical files; a successful comparison that finds a difference still reports 1, by design.

options.text: No — but only because `.conf` files always trigger status 2 regardless of content

options.text: Yes — `&&` requires exit status 1 specifically to run the next command, so a `diff` that finds differences is exactly what should have triggered the echo
options.why: `&&` runs the next command only on exit status 0; status 1 is exactly what causes `&&` to skip the following command, which is the behaviour observed here.

items.rationale: `diff`'s exit status is 0 when the files are identical, 1 when they differ, and 2 on trouble — a difference correctly makes `diff a b && echo same` skip the echo, which is the expected outcome, not a bug.

items.stem: A rescue shell on a server that will not boot offers exactly one editor, and an operator needs to comment out a bad line in an fstab entry and save. Starting from vi's normal mode, what sequence gets the change saved without leaving the file in a broken state?

options.text: Press `i` to insert, edit the line, press Escape, then type `:wq`
options.why: vi starts in normal mode where every key is a command; `i` enters insert mode to make the edit, Escape returns to normal mode, and `:wq` from normal mode writes the file and quits.

options.why: If the editor is still in insert mode, those four characters are inserted into the file as literal text instead of being read as a command; Escape must return to normal mode first.

options.text: Press `a` to append, edit the line, then type `:q!` to save
options.why: `:q!` quits discarding all changes; the command that writes and quits is `:wq`, so this sequence would discard the edit rather than saving it.

options.text: Use `nano`'s `Ctrl-O` and `Ctrl-X` sequence, since it also works inside vi
options.why: nano's key bindings are specific to nano; vi is modal and uses its own normal-mode commands, not nano's Control-key shortcuts.

items.rationale: vi starts in normal mode, where `i` enters insert mode to make changes and Escape returns to normal mode. items.stem: A nightly job takes `tar czf` snapshots of `/var/log/app` and keeps them as the sole recovery mechanism. Comparing archiving against an actual backup strategy, what is missing from relying on archives alone?

options.text: An archive is a one-off bundle at a point in time, not a managed, retained set of independent recovery copies
options.why: Archiving with `tar` bundles files into one stream, but a backup strategy also needs retention, verification and a restore plan across multiple points in time — properties an ad hoc nightly `tar` alone does not guarantee.

options.text: Nothing is missing; a nightly `tar` archive already satisfies every backup requirement
options.why: Treating an archive as automatically equivalent to a full backup strategy overlooks retention and restore planning, which is exactly the confusable pair this scenario is built around.

options.text: The job would need to switch to `zip` instead of `tar` to count as a real backup
options.why: The archive format is not the issue — `zip` also bundles and compresses without addressing retention or restore planning any more than `tar` does.

options.text: Archives cannot be restored at all; only continuous replication to a second host produces recoverable data, because `tar` removes the originals as it bundles them
options.why: A `tar` archive is fully restorable with `tar xzf`, and `tar` does not remove the files it archives - `--remove-files` is a separate opt-in option; the gap this scenario is about is retention and a documented recovery process, not restorability.

Compressing a single stream on its own, independent of tar, is the job of `gzip`; unpacking a zip container instead of a tar archive is `unzip`.

items.stem: An operator writes `tar -cfz logs.tar.gz /var/log`, with a leading hyphen, intending to create a gzip-compressed archive. What does GNU tar actually do with that command line?

options.text: It takes the letter `z` as the archive name, because in a hyphenated cluster the option that needs an argument has to come last
options.why: In UNIX short-option style GNU tar clusters only options that take no argument, with an argument-taking option "at the end of such a cluster, e.g. -vkpf a.tar"; `-cfz` puts `f` before `z`, so `f` consumes `z` as the archive name and `logs.tar.gz` is then read as a path to archive.

options.text: A correctly gzip-compressed `logs.tar.gz`, because GNU tar reorders the letters of a cluster before it parses them
options.why: GNU tar does not reorder a hyphenated cluster; `f` takes the next word in cluster order, which here is the letter `z` itself. Without the leading hyphen this would be traditional style, where "the arguments are read in the same order as the option letters" and `tar cfz logs.tar.gz /var/log` does work.

options.text: An uncompressed archive correctly named `logs.tar.gz`, because a cluster silently drops any letter placed after the one that takes an argument
options.why: Nothing is dropped: `z` is consumed as `f`'s argument, so the file GNU tar creates is named `z`, and `logs.tar.gz` is treated as an input path it then fails to stat.

options.text: A zip-format archive rather than a tar archive, because `z` selects the zip container whenever it follows `f`
options.why: `z` selects gzip compression for a tar archive and never switches to the unrelated zip format; here it is not acting as an option at all, having been consumed as `f`'s argument.

items.rationale: Clustering only applies to short options that take no argument, and the option that takes a value must come last in the cluster, which is why `tar czf` works and `tar cfz` does not — writing `f` before its value is expected breaks the intended result.

The arguments are read in the same order as the option letters" - GNU tar's own example is `tar cfv etc.tar /etc`, with `f` ahead of `v` - whereas the last-in-cluster rule belongs to UNIX short-option style: "Options that take arguments ... can appear at the end of such a cluster, e.g. -vkpf a.tar". No second correct answer; no duplicate options; verdict confirmed.

items.stem: Before extracting an unfamiliar archive with `tar xzf`, an operator wants to know whether it will unpack into its own subdirectory or scatter its files across the current directory. Which habit answers that safely, without extracting anything yet?

options.why: `t` lists the archive's members without extracting them, which reveals whether they are stored under a leading path component — unpacking into a subdirectory — or as bare filenames that would scatter across the current directory.

options.text: Running `gzip -l` on the archive to preview its member list
options.why: `gzip -l` reports compressed and uncompressed size information about a `.gz` stream; it does not list a tar archive's individual member files.

options.why: Listing first with `tar tzf` answers the question without extracting anything at all, which is safer and faster than a trial extraction.

options.text: Running `file` on the archive to read its internal directory structure
options.why: `file` reports the archive's overall type from its magic bytes, such as "gzip compressed data"; it does not enumerate the individual paths stored inside.

items.rationale: An archive whose members are stored with a leading path component unpacks into that directory, while one built from bare filenames scatters them across the current directory — listing first with `tar tzf` is the habit that reveals which case applies before anything is extracted.

items.stem: A nightly job needs to synchronise a large directory tree where only a small fraction changes each night. Comparing `scp` and `rsync` for this repeated task, which is preferred, and why?

options.text: `rsync`, because it compares both ends and transfers only the differences
options.why: `rsync` compares source and destination first and sends only what changed, which makes repeated runs of a mostly-unchanged tree far cheaper than `scp` or `sftp`, which always send the whole file regardless of what already exists at the far end.

options.text: `scp`, because it authenticates faster than `rsync` on repeated connections
options.why: Both tools authenticate exactly as an SSH login does; the deciding factor for a repeated sync is delta transfer, which `scp` does not perform at all.

options.text: Either tool is equally efficient, since both ultimately use SSH as their transport
options.why: Sharing a transport does not make them equally efficient for repeated syncs; only `rsync` compares both ends first to avoid re-sending unchanged data.

options.text: `sftp`, because its interactive session caches previously transferred files
options.why: `sftp` transfers whole files just like `scp`, with no caching of previous transfers that would let it skip unchanged content.

items.rationale: `rsync` compares source and destination first and transfers only what differs, which is what makes repeated runs cheap. `scp` and `sftp` always send the whole file regardless of what is already at the far end. The invocation behind that delta transfer is `rsync -av`.

items.stem: Comparing `rsync -av src/ user@host:/srv/dest/` against the same command with the trailing slash on `src` removed, what is the difference in where the files land?

options.text: With the slash, the contents of `src` land directly inside `dest`; without it, a nested `dest/src` is created
options.why: The trailing slash on the source is significant: `rsync -av src/ dest/` copies the *contents* of `src` into `dest`, while `rsync -av src dest/` creates `dest/src` instead.

options.text: Without the slash, rsync refuses to run and reports a syntax error, because a trailing slash on the source is mandatory whenever the destination is remote
options.why: Both forms are valid rsync invocations against a remote destination; there is no syntax error and no mandatory slash, only a difference in where the transferred files land.

options.text: The slash only affects whether `--delete` is honoured on the destination
options.why: `--delete` behaviour is a separate, unrelated flag; the trailing slash specifically governs whether the source directory's name is nested into the destination.

items.rationale: The trailing slash on the source is significant: `rsync -av src/ dest/` copies the contents of `src` into `dest`, while `rsync -av src dest/` creates `dest/src` — a frequent cause of an unexpectedly nested directory on the first run.

items.stem: A `ping` to a remote host times out. An operator concludes the host is down. What can and cannot actually be concluded from a failed `ping`?

options.text: Nothing conclusive, since ICMP is commonly filtered and a healthy host can still fail to answer echo requests
options.why: `ping` proves reachability when it succeeds, but failure proves neither reachability nor unreachability, because ICMP echo requests are very commonly filtered by firewalls even when the actual service answers fine.

options.text: The host is definitely down, since `ping` failure always means the target is unreachable, because echo replies come from the kernel and cannot be filtered en route
options.why: Echo replies are ordinary IP traffic and are filtered by firewalls routinely; a healthy host behind such a filter answers its real services while never answering `ping`.

options.text: DNS resolution has failed, since `ping` relies entirely on name resolution succeeding first
options.why: A `ping` against an address that resolved fine can still time out due to ICMP filtering; the failure described does not by itself indicate a DNS problem.

options.text: The local network interface is down, since a working interface always gets an ICMP reply
options.why: A working local interface says nothing about whether a distant firewall permits ICMP through to it; the timeout does not localise the problem to the operator's own interface.

items.rationale: `ping` sends ICMP echo requests, so success proves the host is reachable and ICMP is permitted; failure proves neither, because ICMP is very commonly filtered while the actual service still answers fine. The same ladder includes `ip addr` for interface addresses, `ip route` for the routing table, and `hostname` for the system's own name.

items.stem: `dig app.internal` returns the correct address, but the application on the same host still fails to resolve the same name. Where should the investigation look, given what `dig` does and does not consult?

options.text: `/etc/hosts` and the resolver configuration, since `dig` queries DNS directly and skips them
options.why: dig queries the DNS servers listed in `/etc/resolv.conf` directly and never consults `/etc/hosts`, while an application resolves through the `hosts` line of `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, whose sources - typically `files` (that is, `/etc/hosts`) and `dns` - are consulted in the order that line gives; `getent hosts` shows the resulting system view.

options.text: The DNS server itself, since a successful `dig` proves the server is misconfigured
options.why: A successful `dig` result means the DNS server answered correctly; it does not implicate the server, and instead points at the gap between `dig`'s direct query and the application's system-level resolution order.

options.text: The application's TCP port bindings, since `dig` and name resolution are unrelated to sockets
options.why: Nothing in the scenario mentions socket binding; the described failure is specifically about name resolution, which `ss -tulpn` — not `dig` — would investigate if ports were the concern.

options.text: Nowhere further — a successful `dig` result guarantees the application will resolve the name too
options.why: That assumption is exactly the false conclusion this scenario is built to expose; `dig` bypasses `/etc/hosts` and nsswitch, so its success does not guarantee the application's resolution will succeed.

items.rationale: `dig` queries DNS servers directly and skips `/etc/hosts` entirely, whereas the application follows the order in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, which normally consults `/etc/hosts` first — `getent hosts` shows the system's actual resolution order.

items.stem: An operator needs to confirm which process is listening on TCP port 8080 on a server, with numeric ports rather than looked-up service names. Which command and options answer that directly?

options.text: `ss -tulpn`, filtered by eye to the 8080 line
options.why: `ss -tulpn` lists TCP and UDP listening sockets with their owning process and numeric port numbers — `t` TCP, `u` UDP, `l` listening only, `p` process, `n` numeric — which is exactly the "who is listening on which port" answer.

options.text: `curl -I` against the port, since header output reveals the owning process
options.why: `curl -I` fetches HTTP response headers if a service answers; it says nothing about which process on the host is bound to the port, and requires a service to already be responding.

options.text: `traceroute` to the loopback address, since it maps every listening port along the way
options.why: `traceroute` maps the network path to a destination hop by hop; it has no way to enumerate which local processes are listening on which ports.

options.text: `hostname -I`, since it lists every port currently open on the machine
options.why: `hostname -I` shows configured addresses, not port or process information; it does not list listening sockets at all.

items.rationale: `ss -tulpn` lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with ports and owning processes: `t` TCP, `u` UDP, `l` listening, `p` process, `n` numeric so no service-name lookup happens — exactly what is needed to confirm what is bound to 8080.

verification.reasoning: CHECKS every letter of the key against ss(8): `-t, --tcp` "Display TCP sockets"; `-u, --udp` "Display UDP sockets"; `-l, --listening` "Display only listening sockets (these are omitted by default)"; `-p, --processes` "Show processes using sockets"; `-n, --numeric` "Do not try to resolve service names". All five expansions in the key's `why` are the man page's own wording, and together they are exactly the stem's request - owning process, numeric ports, listening only. No second correct answer; no duplicate options. Confirmed as authored.

items.stem: A web server process running as an unprivileged user can bind port 8080 but is refused when it tries port 80. What determines that boundary, and what would let the same process bind 80 without running as root?

options.text: Ports below 1024 need the `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` capability, which can be granted to the binary without making it root
options.why: On Linux only a process holding `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` may bind a port below 1024; that capability can be granted to a specific binary or systemd unit, letting a modern web server bind port 80 while still running unprivileged.

options.text: The boundary is 8080 itself; any port above it needs no privilege and any port below it always does
options.why: The actual privileged boundary is 1024, not 8080; ports from 1024 up to 49151 are registered but unprivileged, so plenty of ports below 8080 need no special capability at all.

options.text: Only the root user account can ever bind port 80, with no exceptions on Linux
options.why: The `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` capability specifically allows binding a privileged port without the process running as root at all, which is exactly how modern web servers avoid running as root.

options.text: The distinction is enforced only by the firewall and not by the kernel, so flushing the firewall rules would let any user bind port 80
options.why: The restriction is a kernel capability check performed at bind time - ip(7) gives EACCES for "binding to a privileged port without superuser privileges (the CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability)" - so it holds with no firewall rules present at all.

items.rationale: Binding a port below 1024 requires the `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` capability on Linux, usually held by root but grantable to a specific binary or systemd unit — which is exactly why an unprivileged process can bind 8080 but not 80 unless it holds that capability.

items.stem: Comparing the RFC's dynamic port range against what a real Linux client actually uses for its outgoing source port, are they the same range?

options.text: No — RFC 6335 puts dynamic ports at 49152-65535, while Linux's default local range is 32768-60999
options.why: The kernel's `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` defaults to 32768 through 60999, not the RFC's 49152-65535, so a real Linux client's source port usually falls inside the registered range rather than the dynamic one.

options.text: Yes — Linux follows RFC 6335's ephemeral range exactly for outgoing connections
options.why: Linux's actual default range diverges from the RFC; this is precisely the specification-versus-implementation gap the topic tests.

options.text: No — Linux uses a narrower range entirely inside the well-known ports, 0-1023
options.why: Linux's ephemeral source-port range sits well above 1023, in the registered-port territory (32768-60999 by default), not inside the privileged well-known range.

options.text: The two ranges differ only for UDP and match exactly for TCP, since the kernel's local port range is consulted only for connectionless sockets
options.why: The kernel documentation defines ip_local_port_range as "the local port range that is used by TCP and UDP to choose the local port" - one setting covering both, so it is not protocol-specific in the way this option claims.

items.rationale: RFC 6335 puts dynamic ports at 49152-65535, but the kernel's `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` defaults to 32768-60999, so a real Linux client's source port usually falls in the User (registered) Ports range instead of the RFC's Dynamic Ports range.

items.stem: `ss -tulpn` is run without the `n` flag, and the output shows a service name instead of a raw port number for a listening socket. What does dropping `n` actually change, and is the resulting name proof of what is running?

options.text: It maps the port number to a name from `/etc/services`, a lookup describing convention, not a check of the actual process
options.why: ss(8) documents `-n, --numeric` as "Do not try to resolve service names", so dropping it lets ss look the port number up in the system's service list; services(5) describes that file as "a mapping between human-friendly textual names for internet services, and their underlying assigned port numbers" - a naming convention, not an inspection of what is actually bound there.

options.text: Nothing changes; `n` only affects whether IP addresses are shown numerically
options.why: `n` governs numeric ports as well as addresses; dropping it specifically substitutes a looked-up service name for the raw port number.

options.text: It disables the `p` column, hiding the owning process entirely
options.why: `n` and `p` are independent flags; dropping `n` changes how ports are displayed, not whether the owning-process column appears.

options.text: It switches the tool from TCP sockets to UDP sockets only, leaving the listening filter and the process column as they were
options.why: Protocol selection is controlled by the separate `t` and `u` flags; `n` has nothing to do with which protocol's sockets are shown.

items.rationale: Dropping `n` and reading the service name from `/etc/services` as proof of what is running is a standing trap: the name is a lookup of the conventional use of that number, not an inspection of the actual process bound to it.
